title: LangChain essentials
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: Runnables and LCEL, prompt templates and structured output, the tool-calling loop, retrievers, loaders and splitters, and tracing with LangSmith or Langfuse.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: What does prompt | model | parser build in LangChain Expression Language (LCEL)?

options.text: A runnable sequence, each output feeding the next, callable via invoke, stream or batch.
options.why: Right: the pipe operator composes Runnables into one Runnable.

options.text: A bitwise OR of three strings that is evaluated once when the module is imported.
options.why: The pipe is overloaded on Runnables; it does not combine strings.

options.text: Three steps run concurrently on the same input, with the first result returned.
options.why: A pipe is sequential: each step waits for the previous output.

options.text: A subclass of a legacy Chain class that you must extend before it can run.
options.why: LCEL composes ordinary Runnables with no subclassing required.

questions.explanation: Composition through the shared Runnable interface is the core idea. Interview takeaway: the same chain supports sync, async, streaming and batch calls.

questions.prompt: A chain composed with LCEL exposes the same Runnable methods as its parts, so one chain can be called on a single input, streamed, or run over a list of inputs.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: invoke, stream and batch (plus async variants) come from the Runnable interface.

options.text: False
options.why: The composed chain is itself a Runnable, so these methods are available.

questions.explanation: Because everything is a Runnable, you can swap a model, add a parser or wrap with retries without changing how callers invoke it.

questions.prompt: You need a validated Pydantic object from a chat model that supports tool calling. Which LangChain approach is the idiomatic one?

options.text: Call the model's with_structured_output with the Pydantic class and use the returned instance.
options.why: Right: it binds the schema and returns parsed, validated data.

options.text: Ask for free text, then run a regex and hope each field is found in the same place.
options.why: Regex parsing is brittle and skips schema validation.

options.text: Use a string parser and call json.loads on whatever comes back without any checking.
options.why: Invalid or partial JSON will raise or pass unchecked data on.

options.text: Set temperature to 0, which guarantees that the output always matches the schema exactly.
options.why: Low temperature does not guarantee schema conformance; validation still matters.

questions.explanation: Structured output uses tool calling or provider JSON modes under the hood. Keep validation and a bounded retry path for the failures that remain.

questions.prompt: You bind_tools to a chat model and it replies with a tool call for get_weather. Who actually runs get_weather?

options.text: Your code or an agent runtime, which sends the result back as a tool message.
options.why: Right: the model only requests the call; execution happens on your side.

options.text: The model provider runs your Python function on its servers and returns the final answer.
options.why: Providers never run your private functions; they only see the schema.

options.text: The model runs it inside its forward pass, because the function name was in the prompt.
options.why: A model generates tokens; it cannot execute code by itself.

options.text: bind_tools registers the function so the model call runs it before returning any message.
options.why: bind_tools only attaches schemas; it does not execute anything.

questions.explanation: The loop is: model emits tool call, your code executes, result goes back as a tool message, and the model continues. This is where you validate arguments and enforce permissions.

questions.prompt: A document loader is the component that splits long documents into chunks sized for the embedding model.

options.text: True
options.why: Loaders only read sources.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: loaders read sources (files, web, databases) into Document objects; text splitters do the chunking.

questions.explanation: Pipeline: load, split, embed, store, retrieve. Keeping the stages separate lets you tune chunk size without touching ingestion.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about chunk size and overlap in a text splitter are correct?

options.text: Larger chunks keep more context but dilute the embedding and use more prompt tokens.
options.why: Right: it is a precision versus context trade-off.

options.text: Overlap reduces the chance that an idea is cut at a boundary, at the cost of duplicated text.
options.why: Right: more overlap means a larger index and some repeated retrieval.

options.text: The best chunk size should be tuned against retrieval evals on your own documents.
options.why: Right: no universal value exists; measure recall on real questions.

options.text: Smaller chunks always retrieve better because every embedding becomes more precise.
options.why: Tiny chunks lose context and can split answers across pieces.

options.text: Overlap should equal the chunk size so that no boundary can ever lose information.
options.why: That duplicates nearly everything and bloats cost without benefit.

questions.explanation: Typical practice is a few hundred to a thousand tokens or characters with modest overlap, but treat that as a starting point to evaluate, not a rule.

questions.prompt: A production RAG answer is wrong. You want the exact retrieved chunks, the final prompt, latency and token counts for that request. What do you need in place?

options.text: Tracing via callbacks, such as LangSmith or Langfuse, recording every step's inputs and outputs.
options.why: Right: a trace links the request to each retrieval, prompt and model call.

options.text: Only application logs of the final answer text, since retrieved chunks are not worth storing.
options.why: Without intermediate steps you cannot tell retrieval faults from generation faults.

options.text: Rerun the question locally at temperature 0 and assume the same chunks and prompt appear.
options.why: Data, index and prompt versions may differ, so local reruns may not reproduce it.

options.text: Increase chunk size globally so that wrong answers become less common over time.
options.why: Guessing a tuning change is not diagnosis; you need evidence first.

questions.explanation: Traces let you separate retrieval errors from generation errors and feed failing cases into your eval dataset. Redact sensitive data before sending traces to a hosted service if policy requires it.

questions.prompt: To improve recall, a team raises the retriever's k from 4 to 20 chunks passed to the model. What is the main cost to expect?

options.text: More prompt tokens, so higher cost and latency, plus a risk that irrelevant chunks distract the model.
options.why: Right: extra context is paid for and can dilute the answer.

options.text: The vector index must be rebuilt, because k is stored as part of the embeddings.
options.why: k is a query-time setting; the index is unaffected.

options.text: The embeddings become less accurate, since more neighbours blur the vectors themselves.
options.why: Embeddings are computed per chunk and do not depend on k.

options.text: No cost at all, since the model only reads chunks that are relevant to the question.
options.why: The model receives whatever you pass, and you are billed for all of it.

questions.explanation: A common pattern is retrieving a larger candidate set, then reranking or filtering down to a few chunks before prompting.
